q: What is the difference between a Pod, a ReplicaSet and a Deployment, and why do you almost never create bare Pods?
p: A Pod is the smallest runnable unit, a ReplicaSet keeps N identical Pods alive, and a Deployment manages ReplicaSets so you get rolling updates and rollbacks. A bare Pod is not rescheduled if its node dies.
tip: Say the ownership chain out loud: Deployment owns ReplicaSet owns Pod. It shows you understand where rollouts really happen.
a: A Pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or more containers sharing network and storage. A ReplicaSet watches a label selector and makes sure a fixed number of identical Pods exist, recreating any that disappear. A Deployment sits above that. It owns ReplicaSets, and each change to the pod template creates a new ReplicaSet while the old one scales down, which is how rolling updates and rollbacks work. The chain is Deployment owns ReplicaSet owns Pod. I almost never create bare Pods in production because nothing recreates them if the node fails or someone drains it. The exceptions are throwaway debugging pods and static pods managed by the kubelet. For stateless apps I use a Deployment, for stable identity and storage a StatefulSet, for one per node a DaemonSet, and for batch work a Job. In an interview I would also mention revisionHistoryLimit, because old ReplicaSets are what rollback uses.
f: Where is rollback history stored?
What does revisionHistoryLimit control?

q: What are the Kubernetes QoS classes and how do they decide who gets evicted first?
p: Guaranteed means every container has requests equal to limits for CPU and memory. Burstable means at least one request or limit is set. BestEffort means none are set. Under node pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable pods exceeding requests, and Guaranteed last.
tip: Mention that QoS is derived, not configured, and that the OOM killer also uses it through oom_score_adj.
a: QoS class is derived from the resource requests and limits on your containers, you do not set it directly. Guaranteed means every container sets CPU and memory requests equal to limits. Burstable means at least one request or limit is set but the pod does not meet the Guaranteed rule. BestEffort means nothing is set at all. It matters when a node runs short of memory or disk. The kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods that use more than they requested, and Guaranteed pods last. The same ordering feeds the Linux OOM score, so a Guaranteed pod is the last the kernel kills. For critical services I set requests equal to limits on memory at least, which gives predictable behaviour. For ordinary services I set realistic requests and a memory limit, and I am careful with CPU limits because they cause throttling.
f: Why can CPU limits hurt latency?
How does the kubelet pick pods to evict?

q: How do Namespaces, ResourceQuota and LimitRange work together to share a cluster fairly?
p: A Namespace is the scope. ResourceQuota caps the total a namespace can consume or create, and LimitRange sets per-pod or per-container defaults and bounds, so a pod without requests still gets sensible ones.
tip: A quota on CPU or memory forces every pod to declare them, so pair it with a LimitRange default or deployments will be rejected.
a: A Namespace gives you a scope for names, RBAC and policies. ResourceQuota limits the aggregate: total CPU and memory requests, number of pods, services, PVCs, even object counts. LimitRange works at the individual object level. It sets default requests and limits, plus minimum and maximum values per container or pod, so a team cannot create a single huge pod or a pod with no limits. They work together. If a ResourceQuota covers CPU or memory, every new pod must specify them or be rejected, and a LimitRange default is what makes that painless. I use this for multi-team clusters: one namespace per team or environment, a quota sized to their budget, a LimitRange with sane defaults, and a NetworkPolicy plus RBAC on top. Namespaces alone are not a security boundary, so for hard isolation I would add policy engines or separate clusters.
f: Is a namespace a security boundary?
What happens when a quota is exceeded?

q: Compare ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName Services. When do you pick each?
p: ClusterIP is internal only. NodePort opens a port on every node. LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer in front of a NodePort. ExternalName is only a DNS CNAME to something outside the cluster.
tip: Add that most production traffic enters through one Ingress or Gateway rather than one cloud load balancer per Service, because of cost.
a: ClusterIP is the default: a stable virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster, which is what service-to-service traffic uses. NodePort opens the same high port on every node and forwards to the Service, useful for simple tests or when an external load balancer is managed by hand. LoadBalancer builds on NodePort and asks the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer, so each Service gets its own cloud resource and cost. ExternalName is different, it creates a DNS CNAME to an outside hostname and does no proxying. In production I keep most Services as ClusterIP and expose a small number of entry points through an Ingress controller or Gateway API, so one load balancer serves many hosts and paths. I use a dedicated LoadBalancer Service for non-HTTP traffic such as TCP or UDP workloads.
f: How does externalTrafficPolicy change the source IP?
When is a headless Service useful?

q: Name the control plane components and describe what each one does.
p: kube-apiserver is the only front door and talks to etcd. etcd stores state. kube-scheduler assigns pods to nodes. kube-controller-manager runs reconciliation loops. cloud-controller-manager talks to the cloud API. On nodes, kubelet and kube-proxy do the work.
tip: Stress that every component talks only to the API server, never to each other directly. That one fact explains most debugging paths.
a: The kube-apiserver is the single entry point. It authenticates and authorises requests, runs admission, validates objects and persists them to etcd. etcd is the consistent key-value store that holds all cluster state. The kube-scheduler watches for unscheduled pods and picks a node by filtering and scoring. The kube-controller-manager runs the reconciliation loops, such as the ReplicaSet, Node, Job and EndpointSlice controllers, each pushing actual state toward desired state. The cloud-controller-manager handles cloud-specific work such as load balancers and node lifecycle. On every node the kubelet runs pods through the container runtime and reports status, and kube-proxy or an eBPF replacement programs Service routing. The key idea is that components only talk through the API server, so if something looks stuck I start by checking the API server and the relevant controller logs.
f: What happens if the scheduler is down?
Which component creates the pods of a Deployment?

q: ConfigMap as environment variables versus as a mounted volume: which one updates live, and what are the consequences?
p: Environment variables are read at container start and never change. Mounted ConfigMap files are refreshed by the kubelet within a minute or so, except when mounted with subPath, which never updates.
tip: Mention a checksum annotation on the pod template, a common Helm trick, to force a rollout when the config changes.
a: When a ConfigMap is injected as environment variables, the values are copied into the container at startup, so changing the ConfigMap does nothing until the pod is restarted. When it is mounted as a volume, the kubelet eventually updates the files, usually within a minute, using an atomic symlink swap. The catch is that the application must reload the file itself, and a subPath mount never updates at all. Because of this I choose based on the app. If it supports hot reload, I mount the volume. Otherwise I prefer immutable config and trigger a rollout whenever it changes, for example with a checksum annotation in the pod template or a tool such as Reloader. Making ConfigMaps immutable also reduces API server load and avoids accidental live changes. I treat config changes like code changes: versioned, reviewed and rolled out gradually.
f: Why does subPath break updates?
What does an immutable ConfigMap give you?

q: What are the postStart and preStop lifecycle hooks, and how do they interact with graceful shutdown?
p: postStart runs right after the container is created, without any ordering guarantee against the entrypoint. preStop runs before SIGTERM is sent and is used to drain connections. Both count toward terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
tip: A short sleep in preStop is a common fix for 502s during rollouts, because endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other.
a: Lifecycle hooks let you run a command or HTTP call at two points. postStart fires immediately after the container starts, but it runs alongside the main process and there is no guarantee it finishes first, so I avoid depending on it. preStop runs when the pod is being terminated, before the container receives SIGTERM, and it is the right place to stop accepting new work and drain in-flight requests. The sequence is: the pod is marked Terminating, it is removed from Service endpoints, preStop runs, SIGTERM is sent, and after terminationGracePeriodSeconds the kubelet sends SIGKILL. The grace period includes the preStop time. The classic production issue is that endpoint removal and shutdown race, so clients still hit a pod that is closing. A short sleep in preStop, plus an app that handles SIGTERM properly, usually fixes dropped requests during deployments.
f: Why do users see 502s during a rollout?
What happens if preStop exceeds the grace period?

q: How does kubectl rollout undo work, and where are revisions stored?
p: Each pod-template change creates a new ReplicaSet, and the Deployment keeps old ones up to revisionHistoryLimit. Undo scales an old ReplicaSet back up and the current one down. Scaling or changing replicas alone does not create a revision.
tip: In a GitOps setup, prefer reverting the commit. A manual undo will be overwritten at the next sync.
a: A Deployment stores its history as ReplicaSets. Every change to the pod template, such as a new image or env var, creates a new ReplicaSet with a revision annotation. Old ReplicaSets are kept at zero replicas, up to revisionHistoryLimit, which defaults to ten. kubectl rollout undo simply scales an earlier ReplicaSet back up and the current one down using the same rolling update strategy, so it is safe and gradual. Changing replica count alone does not create a revision, because it does not touch the template. Adding a change-cause annotation makes the history readable. One thing I always call out is GitOps: if Argo CD or Flux manages the Deployment, a manual undo drifts from Git and will be reverted, so the correct rollback is to revert the commit. Also remember that rollback does not undo database migrations.
f: Does rollback restore ConfigMaps?
What if revisionHistoryLimit is zero?

q: Explain how a Helm chart is structured and what helm template, helm upgrade --install and helm diff are for.
p: A chart has Chart.yaml, values.yaml and a templates folder. helm template renders manifests locally with no cluster. helm upgrade --install is idempotent deploy. helm diff, a plugin, shows what would change before you apply.
tip: Use --atomic or --wait in CI so a failed release rolls itself back instead of leaving a half-deployed state.
a: A Helm chart packages Kubernetes manifests as Go templates. Chart.yaml holds metadata and dependencies, values.yaml holds defaults, and the templates folder holds the manifests plus helpers. A release is an installed instance of a chart, with its history stored as Secrets in the namespace. helm template renders the manifests locally without touching a cluster, which is ideal for linting, policy checks and reviewing what will be applied. helm upgrade with the install flag is the idempotent command pipelines use: it installs if the release does not exist and upgrades otherwise. The diff plugin compares the proposed release to what is live, which I want in every pull request. In CI I use atomic and a timeout so a failed upgrade rolls back automatically. For environments, I keep one chart with a values file per environment, and pin chart versions rather than using latest.
f: Where does Helm store release state?
When would you choose Kustomize instead?

q: What is an EndpointSlice, and why did it replace the Endpoints object?
p: Endpoints stored every pod IP of a Service in one object, so a change to one pod rewrote and resent the whole thing to every node. EndpointSlices shard that into small chunks, default 100 endpoints each, which scales far better.
tip: Mention that kube-proxy and the ingress controllers now watch EndpointSlices, so large Services update much faster.
a: The original Endpoints object held every backend address for a Service in a single resource. In a Service with thousands of pods, each pod change rewrote that large object and pushed it to every node watching it, which created API server and network load. EndpointSlices fix this by splitting the addresses into multiple small objects, by default up to a hundred endpoints each. Only the affected slice is updated and sent. They also carry richer data such as ready, serving and terminating conditions, node name and topology zone, which supports features like topology-aware routing and graceful termination. kube-proxy, Cilium and most ingress controllers now consume EndpointSlices. For day-to-day debugging I still check that a Service has endpoints, and if the list is empty I look at the selector, the pod labels and readiness.
f: What does it mean if a Service has no endpoints?
How does topology-aware routing use slices?

q: How do you manage access to multiple clusters with kubeconfig contexts without making mistakes?
p: A kubeconfig holds clusters, users and contexts. A context binds one cluster, one user and a default namespace. Switch with kubectl config use-context, or better, use the KUBECONFIG variable per shell and a prompt that shows the context.
tip: Name a real habit: a coloured prompt for prod, and short-lived credentials from SSO or an exec plugin rather than static tokens.
a: A kubeconfig file contains three lists: clusters with their API endpoints and CA, users with their credentials, and contexts that tie a cluster, a user and a default namespace together. The risk with several clusters is running a command against the wrong one. My habits are to show the current context and namespace in the shell prompt, colour production differently, pass the context explicitly in scripts with the context flag, and keep separate kubeconfig files per environment selected with the KUBECONFIG variable. For authentication I avoid long-lived static tokens and use the cloud provider's exec plugin or OIDC login so credentials are short-lived and tied to a person. I also use RBAC so day-to-day access to production is read-only, with elevated access granted just in time. Tools like kubectx help, but the safeguard is process, not tooling.
f: How do you give temporary admin access?
Why avoid static tokens in kubeconfig?

q: When do you use kubectl debug node, and how is it different from SSH to the node?
p: kubectl debug node/<name> starts a privileged pod on that node with the host filesystem mounted at /host. It gives you host-level access without opening SSH, and the access is audited through the API server.
tip: Delete the debug pod afterwards, and mention that on managed or immutable OS nodes this is often the only way in.
a: kubectl debug node creates a pod scheduled on a specific node, with the host's root filesystem mounted under slash host and host namespaces available. From there I can read kubelet and container runtime logs, inspect disk usage, check iptables or conntrack, and chroot into the host if I need host tools. Compared with SSH, there is no need to open port 22 or manage keys, access is authorised through Kubernetes RBAC, and every action starts with an auditable API call. It is also often the only option on managed or immutable node images, such as Bottlerocket or Talos, where SSH is disabled by design. Because the pod is privileged, I restrict who can create it, clean it up when done, and avoid making changes by hand on nodes. Anything I learn goes back into automation or node images.
f: What RBAC permission does this need?
How would you debug a node on Talos?

q: What are static pods, and which cluster components commonly run as static pods?
p: Static pods are defined as manifest files in a directory on a node, and the kubelet runs them directly with no API server involved. A mirror pod is created in the API so you can see them. kubeadm control plane components use this.
tip: This is why you edit a file on the control plane node, not use kubectl edit, to change the API server flags in a kubeadm cluster.
a: Static pods are pods the kubelet manages straight from manifest files in a configured directory, typically slash etc slash kubernetes slash manifests. The kubelet watches the folder, starts the pod, restarts it if it dies, and creates a read-only mirror pod in the API server so it is visible with kubectl. Because they do not depend on the control plane, they solve the bootstrap problem. In a kubeadm cluster the API server, controller manager, scheduler and etcd all run as static pods. To change an API server flag, I edit the manifest on that node and the kubelet recreates the pod, and kubectl edit on the mirror pod will not work. I also use static pods rarely for node-critical agents. The trade-off is that they are not managed by a controller, so there is no rolling update or central management.
f: Why can't you delete a static pod with kubectl?
How would you upgrade control plane flags safely?

q: What do the kubelet and the container runtime each do, and what is CRI?
p: The kubelet is the node agent that makes pods match the spec. It talks to a container runtime such as containerd or CRI-O through the Container Runtime Interface, a gRPC API. Docker Engine support through dockershim was removed in 1.24.
tip: If asked about dockershim, say images built with Docker still run fine, because they are OCI images.
a: The kubelet runs on every node. It watches for pods assigned to its node, asks the runtime to pull images and start containers, runs probes, mounts volumes, reports status and enforces resource limits. It does not run containers itself. It speaks the Container Runtime Interface, a gRPC API, to a runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, and those in turn use a low-level runtime such as runc to create the actual Linux containers. Kubernetes removed the built-in Docker integration, dockershim, in version 1.24, but images built with Docker are standard OCI images and still run. For debugging on a node I use crictl, since the docker command may not exist. The usual failure points are a stopped kubelet, a full disk, runtime socket problems, or certificate expiry, so I check journalctl for the kubelet first.
f: What is the difference between containerd and runc?
How do you list containers on a node without Docker?

q: What does volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer solve, and why does it matter on multi-zone clusters?
p: With Immediate binding, a zonal disk is created before the pod is scheduled, possibly in a zone where the pod cannot run. WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until the pod is scheduled, so the disk is created in the same zone as the node.
cmds: kubectl describe pvc data-0 | grep -i 'waiting for first consumer'
tip: A PVC showing Pending with this mode is normal until a pod uses it. Do not misread it as a failure.
a: Block storage such as EBS or a persistent disk lives in a single availability zone. With Immediate binding, Kubernetes provisions the volume as soon as the PVC is created, before any pod exists, so the scheduler may later be forced to place the pod in a different zone than the disk, leaving the pod stuck Pending with a volume node affinity conflict. WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until a pod that uses the claim is scheduled. The scheduler then considers all the pod's constraints, picks a node, and the volume is created in that node's zone. It matters for multi-zone clusters and StatefulSets. A side effect is that the PVC stays Pending until a pod consumes it, which is expected. I set this mode on every zonal StorageClass, and combine it with topology spread so replicas land in different zones.
f: What is a volume node affinity conflict?
How does this interact with pod anti-affinity?

q: Explain the PersistentVolume access modes: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany and ReadWriteOncePod.
p: RWO allows one node to mount read-write, not one pod. ROX allows many nodes read-only. RWX allows many nodes read-write and needs a shared filesystem such as NFS or EFS. RWOP restricts the volume to a single pod.
tip: Point out the RWO trap: several pods on the same node can still share an RWO volume.
a: Access modes describe how many nodes can use a volume at once, and what they can do. ReadWriteOnce means a single node can mount it read-write. Note that it is per node, not per pod, so multiple pods on the same node can share it. ReadOnlyMany lets many nodes mount it read-only. ReadWriteMany lets many nodes mount it read-write, but block devices cannot do this, so you need a shared file system such as NFS, EFS, Azure Files or CephFS. ReadWriteOncePod restricts it to exactly one pod in the whole cluster and is the right choice when you need strict single-writer safety. The storage backend must support the mode you request or the claim stays Pending. In design reviews I ask whether the app really needs shared writes, because RWX file systems are slower and often the wrong tool for databases.
f: Why does a Deployment with RWO and rolling updates sometimes hang?
Which mode suits a database?

q: What is the PersistentVolume reclaim policy, and when would you choose Retain over Delete?
p: Delete removes the underlying disk when the PVC is deleted, which is the default for dynamic provisioning. Retain keeps the disk and the PV in Released state, so data survives and an admin can recover it.
tip: Say that Retain is not a backup. It only prevents accidental deletion, so you still need snapshots.
a: The reclaim policy decides what happens to the storage when the claim bound to a PersistentVolume is deleted. With Delete, which is the default for dynamically provisioned volumes, the cloud disk is destroyed along with the PVC. That is convenient for dev and test but dangerous in production, because deleting a namespace or a StatefulSet's claims can destroy data. With Retain, the PV moves to a Released state and the disk stays, so an administrator can recover the data, but the volume is not automatically reused and needs manual cleanup or a new PV that references it. For production databases I set Retain on the StorageClass, or patch the PV, and add snapshots and tested restores, since Retain protects against accidental deletion, not corruption or region failure. I also enable protection finalizers so an in-use PVC cannot be removed.
f: How do you reuse a Released volume?
What does the storage-object-in-use protection do?

q: What is the difference between an Ingress resource and an Ingress controller, and how do you terminate TLS?
p: An Ingress resource is only routing rules in the API. An Ingress controller, such as NGINX, Traefik or a cloud ALB controller, watches those rules and configures a real proxy. TLS is terminated at the controller using a certificate stored in a Secret.
tip: Mention that without an installed controller an Ingress object does nothing, which is a common first-day surprise.
a: The Ingress resource is just configuration: hosts, paths and which Service each should go to. By itself it does nothing. An Ingress controller is the running component that watches Ingress objects and programs a real proxy or cloud load balancer, and the IngressClass says which controller owns which Ingress. For TLS, the Ingress references a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls containing the certificate and key, and the controller terminates HTTPS and forwards to pods, often over plain HTTP inside the cluster or re-encrypted if required. I normally automate certificates with cert-manager and Let's Encrypt or a private CA. Ingress is limited to HTTP and relies on annotations for advanced features, so newer designs use the Gateway API, which has clearer roles and richer routing. For TCP or UDP I use a LoadBalancer Service.
f: Why is Gateway API replacing Ingress?
How do you do mTLS at the edge?

q: How does cert-manager issue and renew certificates inside a cluster?
p: You define an Issuer or ClusterIssuer, such as Let's Encrypt or Vault. A Certificate resource, or an annotated Ingress, requests a cert. cert-manager completes the ACME challenge, stores the result in a Secret, and renews it before expiry.
tip: Name the usual failure: the HTTP-01 challenge is blocked by a redirect or a firewall. DNS-01 avoids it and supports wildcards.
a: cert-manager adds custom resources for certificates. An Issuer or ClusterIssuer describes who signs, for example Let's Encrypt through ACME, HashiCorp Vault, or an internal CA. A Certificate resource states the names you need and the Secret to store them in. You can also annotate an Ingress and cert-manager creates the Certificate for you. For ACME it creates an Order and Challenges. HTTP-01 proves control by serving a token over port 80, DNS-01 proves it by creating a DNS record, which also supports wildcard certificates. Once issued, the key and certificate go in a Secret, which Ingress or workloads mount. cert-manager renews automatically, by default when about a third of the lifetime remains. When it fails, I look at the Certificate, CertificateRequest, Order and Challenge events in that order, and alert on expiry as a safety net.
f: When would you choose DNS-01?
How do pods pick up a renewed cert?

q: What are good practices for Kubernetes labels, selectors and annotations?
p: Labels identify and select; annotations hold non-identifying metadata. Use the recommended app.kubernetes.io set, keep selectors stable because Deployment selectors are immutable, and never put secrets or large data in either.
tip: A well-known trap: if a Service selector matches pods from two Deployments, traffic is split between them.
a: Labels are key-value pairs used to group and select objects: Services pick pods, Deployments own ReplicaSets, and policies target workloads, all by label selectors. Annotations hold metadata that tools use but that is never selected on, for example ingress settings, checksums or build information. My practices are to adopt the standard app.kubernetes.io labels for name, instance, version, component and part-of, add ownership and environment labels for cost allocation, keep selector labels minimal and stable because a Deployment's selector is immutable, and avoid putting changing values like the version in the selector. I never store secrets in either, and I keep annotation size modest. A common production bug is overlapping selectors, where a Service or Deployment accidentally adopts pods it should not own, so I review selectors carefully and use unique names per workload.
f: Why is a Deployment selector immutable?
How would you find all pods by team for cost reports?

q: What are native sidecar containers, and how do they differ from the old sidecar pattern?
p: Native sidecars are init containers with restartPolicy Always. They start before the app, keep running alongside it, are restarted independently, and are stopped after the app ends. This fixes ordering and Job completion problems of regular sidecars.
tip: The headline benefit is that a Job with a log or proxy sidecar can now actually complete.
a: Traditionally a sidecar was just another container in the pod's container list. That had two problems: there was no start ordering, so the app could start before the proxy was ready, and in a Job the pod never finished because the sidecar kept running. Native sidecars, enabled by default in recent Kubernetes versions, are declared as init containers with restartPolicy Always. They start in order before the main containers, stay running for the life of the pod, support their own probes, and are terminated after the main containers exit. That makes service mesh proxies, log shippers and credential refreshers behave properly, and lets batch Jobs complete. I would use a sidecar when the helper must share the pod's network or volumes and have the same lifecycle, and choose a separate Deployment or DaemonSet when it is independent.
f: How is this different from a regular init container?
What happens to the sidecar at pod shutdown?

q: Why do many teams remove CPU limits, and what does CFS throttling have to do with it?
p: CPU limits are enforced by the CFS quota in 100 ms periods. A multi-threaded app can use its whole quota in a few milliseconds and then be paused for the rest of the period, which hurts tail latency even when the node is idle.
tip: Keep CPU requests accurate, since requests drive scheduling and fair sharing. Memory limits you should keep.
a: CPU requests set the share a container gets under contention, and the scheduler uses them for placement. A CPU limit is a hard cap enforced by the Linux CFS quota: the container may use a certain amount of CPU time per hundred millisecond period, and once it is spent the threads are paused until the next period. For multi-threaded or bursty applications this means you can be throttled even though the node has idle CPU, which shows up as latency spikes. You can see it in the container CPU throttled periods metric. Because of this, many teams set accurate CPU requests and no CPU limit, letting pods burst into spare capacity, while keeping memory limits because memory cannot be reclaimed safely. The trade-off is noisy neighbours, so I keep requests honest, use Guaranteed class for critical pods, and monitor node saturation.
f: How do you measure throttling?
What is the downside of having no CPU limit?

q: How do you write a default-deny NetworkPolicy that still lets pods resolve DNS?
p: Create an empty podSelector policy with both Ingress and Egress types, then add an egress allow to the kube-dns pods on UDP and TCP 53 in the kube-system namespace. Without that rule, all name lookups break.
tip: Always confirm your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy. Some, like plain Flannel, silently ignore it.
a: By default pods accept traffic from anywhere. To get zero trust I first apply a policy per namespace with an empty pod selector and policy types set to both Ingress and Egress, with no rules, which denies everything. The first thing that breaks is DNS, because egress to CoreDNS is blocked, so I immediately add an egress rule that allows UDP and TCP port 53 to the kube-dns pods in kube-system, selected with a namespace selector and a pod label. Then I add explicit allow policies per application: the frontend can reach the API, the API can reach the database, and the ingress controller can reach the frontend. I test each step with a debug pod. It is vital to check that the CNI actually enforces policies, since some do not, and to remember that policies are additive.
f: How do you allow traffic to a cloud metadata service?
How do you test policies before enforcing them?

q: What is Kubernetes audit logging, and how would you use it to investigate an incident?
p: The API server can record every request according to an audit policy, with levels None, Metadata, Request and RequestResponse. Logs go to a file or webhook, and you query who did what, to which resource, when, and from where.
tip: On managed clusters, enable the provider's control plane logs, because audit is often off by default.
a: Audit logging records requests handled by the API server, each as a structured event with the user, groups, source IP, verb, resource, namespace, response code and time. An audit policy decides what is recorded and at which level: None, Metadata, Request, or RequestResponse. I record Metadata for most things, log secrets only at Metadata so values never reach the logs, and capture more detail for RBAC changes and exec calls. The output goes to a file or a webhook, and from there to a log platform. In an incident I answer questions like who deleted this deployment, who created this cluster role binding, which service account listed secrets, and from which IP. On EKS, GKE and AKS I turn on the managed control plane audit logs, since they are not always enabled. Alerts on exec into pods, privileged pod creation and RBAC changes are valuable.
f: Why not log secrets at RequestResponse?
Which events would you alert on?

q: What is the difference between metrics-server and Prometheus, and where does kubectl top get its data?
p: metrics-server keeps only current CPU and memory in memory for kubectl top and the HPA. It stores no history. Prometheus scrapes many metrics and stores time series for dashboards, alerting and analysis.
tip: If kubectl top fails, check the metrics-server pod and the v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io APIService first.
a: metrics-server is a lightweight aggregator. It scrapes the kubelet's resource metrics endpoint, keeps the latest CPU and memory numbers in memory, and exposes them through the metrics API. That is what kubectl top and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler read. It stores no history and has no application metrics, so it cannot support dashboards or alerting. Prometheus is a full monitoring system: it scrapes targets such as kubelet cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics, node exporters and application endpoints, stores time series, and lets you query with PromQL and fire alerts. For custom or external metrics the HPA needs an adapter such as the Prometheus adapter or KEDA. In production you need both: metrics-server for autoscaling and quick checks, Prometheus for history and alerts. If kubectl top returns an error I check that metrics-server is running and that its APIService is available, then look at kubelet TLS settings.
f: Why does the HPA show unknown for metrics?
What does kube-state-metrics add?

q: What is KEDA, and when would you use it instead of the standard HPA?
p: KEDA scales workloads on event sources such as queue length, Kafka lag or cron schedules, and can scale to zero. It feeds the HPA with external metrics. The plain HPA mostly scales on CPU and memory and cannot go to zero.
tip: Scale-to-zero suits workers, not user-facing APIs, because of cold start latency.
a: The standard HPA scales a workload from resource metrics like CPU and memory, or custom metrics if you add an adapter, and it needs at least one replica. KEDA is an operator that adds event-driven autoscaling. You define a ScaledObject that points at a trigger such as SQS or RabbitMQ queue depth, Kafka consumer lag, a Prometheus query or a cron schedule. KEDA creates and manages an HPA behind the scenes and also handles the zero-to-one activation, so idle workers can scale to zero and cost nothing. I use it for queue consumers and batch workers where load is driven by backlog rather than CPU. I avoid scale to zero for latency-sensitive services because of cold start. Important settings are cooldown periods, polling interval and a sensible maximum replica count so a burst does not overwhelm downstream systems.
f: What happens to in-flight messages at scale-down?
How do you cap downstream load?

q: Pods are being evicted because of DiskPressure on a node. How do you investigate and prevent a repeat?
p: The kubelet evicts pods when nodefs or imagefs falls under its threshold, and also garbage-collects images. Find what is filling the disk: container logs, images, emptyDir, or writable layers.
cmds: kubectl debug node/<n> -it --image=busybox -- du -xh /host/var/lib --max-depth=2 | sort -h | tail
tip: Name three preventers: log rotation limits, ephemeral-storage requests and limits, and image garbage collection thresholds.
a: I start with the node condition and events to confirm DiskPressure, then check which filesystem is affected: the node root, or the image and container storage. Using a debug pod I run du on the container runtime directory and var log to see what is large. Usual culprits are unrotated container logs, a pile of unused images, pods writing big files to emptyDir or their writable layer, and core dumps. Immediate relief is to prune unused images, remove old logs, or cordon and drain the node and replace it. Long term I set container log rotation in the kubelet, set ephemeral-storage requests and limits so a misbehaving pod is evicted rather than the node suffering, tune image garbage collection thresholds, and move heavy temporary data to a proper volume. I also alert on node disk usage before eviction thresholds, so we act at eighty percent, not at the edge.
f: What are the kubelet eviction thresholds?
How do ephemeral-storage limits help?

q: A Deployment rollout finished but some old pods are stuck in Terminating forever. What is going on?
p: A pod stays Terminating when a finalizer blocks it, the node is unreachable so the kubelet cannot confirm deletion, the process ignores SIGTERM and the grace period is very long, or a volume cannot be unmounted.
tip: Force delete is a last resort. For StatefulSets it can allow two pods with the same identity, which risks data corruption.
a: First I look at the pod's deletion timestamp, finalizers, node and events. If the node is NotReady or unreachable, the kubelet cannot report the container as gone, so the pod stays Terminating until the node returns or is removed. If there are finalizers, some controller has not finished its cleanup, so I find that controller and fix it rather than removing the finalizer blindly. If the node is healthy, the application may be ignoring SIGTERM, with a long terminationGracePeriodSeconds, or a volume unmount is hanging, which I see in kubelet logs. Force deleting the pod object removes it from the API but does not guarantee the process is dead, which is dangerous for StatefulSets and volumes. So I only force delete after confirming the node or process is gone. Prevention is handling SIGTERM correctly and keeping sensible grace periods.
f: Why is force delete risky for StatefulSets?
How do you find which controller owns a finalizer?

q: ImagePullBackOff happens only on some nodes, not all. How do you find the cause?
p: If the same image works on some nodes, the problem is node-specific: registry rate limits per IP, missing credentials or a node role without ECR access, DNS or proxy issues on that node, or a full disk.
cmds: crictl pull <image>  # run on the failing node
tip: Docker Hub anonymous pull limits are a classic. Use authenticated pulls or a pull-through cache.
a: The key clue is that the same image works elsewhere, so I focus on what differs per node. I look at which nodes fail and read the pod events for the exact error. A rate limit message points to anonymous Docker Hub pulls shared by a NAT address, so I add imagePullSecrets or a registry mirror. An unauthorized error suggests node credentials, such as a missing ECR policy on one node group's IAM role. A timeout or no such host suggests DNS, proxy, security group or route problems on that subnet. I reproduce on the node using crictl pull, and check disk space, since a full image filesystem also fails pulls. The fix is usually to standardise node roles and networking, use a pull-through cache in our own registry, and pin images by digest so behaviour is consistent.
f: How do you avoid Docker Hub limits at scale?
Why pin images by digest?

q: A Service works from inside the cluster but is unreachable from outside through its NodePort. How do you debug?
p: Check the layers in order: pod readiness and endpoints, kube-proxy rules on the node, cloud security groups or firewall for the port range 30000-32767, externalTrafficPolicy, and whether the node you hit has a local pod.
cmds: kubectl get svc web -o wide; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
tip: With externalTrafficPolicy Local, nodes without a local pod drop the traffic. This is by design and preserves the source IP.
a: I walk from the inside out. First confirm the Service has ready endpoints, because a selector or readiness problem would also break internal access. Since the ClusterIP works, the pods are probably fine, so the problem is the external path. I test the NodePort from another machine on the same network, then from the node itself. If it works locally but not remotely, it is a cloud security group, network ACL or firewall blocking the NodePort range. If one node works and another does not, I check externalTrafficPolicy: with Local, only nodes running a backend pod respond, and the load balancer health check should exclude the others. I also check kube-proxy is running and its rules exist. The fix is opening the right security group rule or switching traffic policy, and for the long term I prefer a managed load balancer or Ingress over raw NodePorts.
f: What does externalTrafficPolicy Cluster do to the client IP?
How does a load balancer health check work with Local?

q: Every pod creation suddenly fails with a webhook timeout or certificate error. What happened and how do you recover?
p: A validating or mutating admission webhook is unreachable or its serving certificate expired, and its failurePolicy is Fail, so the API server rejects all matching requests. Disable or fix the webhook configuration to unblock.
tip: Exempt kube-system and the webhook's own namespace, and set a timeout. The webhook that guards pods must not depend on pods it blocks.
a: This is the classic self-inflicted outage. An admission webhook, for example from Gatekeeper, Kyverno or a service mesh injector, is called by the API server on matching requests. If the webhook pods are down, or the serving certificate expired, and the failure policy is Fail, every matching request is rejected, including the request that would recreate the webhook pods, which creates a deadlock. To recover I list the webhook configurations, find the one whose errors appear in the API server message, and temporarily delete it or set its failure policy to Ignore, then fix the underlying certificate or deployment and restore it. To prevent a repeat, I exclude system namespaces and the webhook's own namespace using namespace selectors, set short timeouts, run multiple replicas with disruption budgets, automate certificate rotation, and alert on webhook latency and error rates.
f: When is failurePolicy Fail appropriate?
How do you roll out a new policy safely?

q: etcd reports 'mvcc: database space exceeded' and the cluster turns read-only. How do you recover?
p: etcd hits its quota, default 2 GB, raises a NOSPACE alarm and only accepts reads and deletes. Compact the history, defragment, then disarm the alarm. Find out what grew: usually events or a controller writing too much.
cmds: rev=$(etcdctl endpoint status -w json | jq '.[0].Status.header.revision'); etcdctl compact $rev
tip: Take a snapshot before you touch anything, and defrag one member at a time because it blocks that member.
a: When the etcd database passes its quota, it raises a NOSPACE alarm and the cluster stops accepting writes, so the API server becomes effectively read-only. First I take a snapshot for safety. Then I compact the key history to the latest revision, which marks old versions as free, defragment each member one at a time to actually return the space, and finally disarm the alarm. Defrag blocks the member while it runs, so I do it sequentially, followers first. Then I investigate the root cause. Common causes are a huge number of Events, a controller or operator that updates objects in a loop, large Secrets or CRs, or leftover Jobs. I fix the source, enable automatic compaction, set an alert on database size, and, if needed, raise the quota modestly. On managed clusters I would open a support ticket because I cannot reach etcd directly.
f: Why isn't compaction enough on its own?
How do you spot which resource type is largest?

q: A pod is stuck in ContainerCreating. What are the likely causes and how do you narrow them down?
p: The pod is scheduled but the kubelet cannot finish setup. Typical causes are a failing volume mount or attach, a missing ConfigMap or Secret, CNI problems assigning an IP, or the runtime failing to pull or create the sandbox.
tip: Events usually name the culprit in one line, such as FailedMount, FailedCreatePodSandBox or FailedAttachVolume.
a: ContainerCreating means the scheduler has done its job and the kubelet is preparing the pod. I go straight to the pod events because they usually give the reason. FailedMount or FailedAttachVolume points to storage: a missing PVC, a volume still attached to another node, a missing Secret or ConfigMap, or a CSI driver problem. FailedCreatePodSandBox often means the CNI plugin could not set up networking, for example because the node ran out of IP addresses or the CNI pod is unhealthy. Slow progress with pulling messages suggests registry or bandwidth problems with large images. If events are quiet, I read kubelet and container runtime logs on the node. Once I know the layer, I fix it, such as correcting the object name, freeing the volume, or replacing a node with exhausted IPs. I would also add alerts for pods stuck longer than a few minutes.
f: What does FailedCreatePodSandBox usually indicate?
How do you check if a CSI driver is healthy?

q: External lookups from pods are slow and some calls take about five seconds. How do ndots and CoreDNS play a role?
p: The default ndots:5 makes the resolver try several search-domain suffixes before the real name, multiplying queries. Combined with the UDP conntrack race, timeouts of 5 seconds appear. Use fully qualified names, tune ndots, and add NodeLocal DNSCache.
tip: A trailing dot on external hostnames, api.example.com., skips the search path entirely.
a: Inside a pod, resolv.conf has several search domains and ndots set to five. Any name with fewer than five dots is first tried with each search suffix, so looking up an external host like api.example.com can trigger several failed queries before the right one, and each failure adds load and latency. If CoreDNS is overloaded, or there is a conntrack race on UDP, a lost packet causes a classic five second timeout. I check CoreDNS CPU and logs, its cache and forward settings, and the resolv.conf. Fixes include using fully qualified names with a trailing dot for external calls, lowering ndots with dnsConfig for chatty workloads, scaling CoreDNS with the cluster proportional autoscaler, and deploying NodeLocal DNSCache so lookups hit a local cache over TCP. I would also measure with dnsperf style tests to confirm the improvement.
f: What is NodeLocal DNSCache?
Why does the UDP race cause 5 second delays?

q: Pods cannot get IP addresses because the node ran out of IPs. How does that happen on EKS and what are the options?
p: With the AWS VPC CNI, each pod uses a real VPC IP drawn from the ENIs attached to the node, so the instance type's ENI and IP limits cap pods per node and small subnets run dry. Use prefix delegation, custom networking or larger subnets.
tip: Say the formula: max pods = ENIs x (IPs per ENI - 1) + 2. It shows you know why small instances fit few pods.
a: The AWS VPC CNI gives each pod a secondary private IP from the node's elastic network interfaces. The instance type limits how many interfaces and addresses it can hold, so it limits the pods per node, and subnets with small CIDR blocks can be exhausted as the cluster grows, leaving pods in ContainerCreating with IP allocation errors. I check the aws-node logs and subnet free address counts. Remedies include enabling prefix delegation, which assigns blocks of sixteen addresses per slot and greatly increases density, using custom networking so pods draw from a secondary CIDR such as the 100.64 range, adding larger subnets, or choosing an overlay or Cilium based networking. I would also right-size the number of nodes and consider IPv6. Long term, I plan pod CIDR capacity at design time and alert when subnets drop below a free address threshold.
f: What is prefix delegation?
How does an overlay network avoid this?

q: A pod fails with 'Multi-Attach error for volume' after a node failure. Why, and how do you resolve it safely?
p: A ReadWriteOnce block volume is still attached to the failed node, so the CSI attacher will not attach it elsewhere until the old attachment is released. Wait for the force-detach timeout, or confirm the node is truly down and remove the VolumeAttachment.
cmds: kubectl delete volumeattachment <name>   # only after node is confirmed gone
tip: Never force the detach while the old node might still be writing. That can corrupt the filesystem.
a: A block volume with ReadWriteOnce can be attached to only one node. When a node dies without cleanly detaching, the VolumeAttachment object still says the disk belongs to it, so when the pod is rescheduled to a new node, the attach fails with a Multi-Attach error. Kubernetes eventually force-detaches after a timeout, around six minutes, once the node is considered unhealthy, and newer versions with non-graceful node shutdown handling can speed that up. Manually, I first confirm the old node is really down or terminated, preferably by stopping or deleting the instance, because if it is still running and writing, detaching risks data corruption. Then I delete the stale VolumeAttachment or the node object so the volume can attach to the new node. For better resilience I use replicated storage or databases with their own replication, instead of depending on one disk.
f: What is non-graceful node shutdown?
How would a StatefulSet recover faster?

q: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler keeps flapping between scale up and scale down. How do you stabilise it?
p: Flapping comes from noisy metrics, short windows, a target near the natural load level, or slow pod startup. Use stabilizationWindowSeconds, scaling policies, a better metric, and readiness so new pods are counted correctly.
cmds: kubectl get hpa web -o yaml | grep -A12 behavior
tip: Scale up fast, scale down slowly is the usual rule. The behavior field lets you set each direction separately.
a: First I watch the HPA events and the metric values to see what triggers each decision. Flapping typically has a few causes. The target utilisation may sit right at the normal operating point, so small changes cross the threshold. The metric may be spiky, like instantaneous CPU. New pods may take long to start, so the average drops, then the HPA scales down, and load rises again. To stabilise I use the behavior section: a longer scale-down stabilization window of five minutes, policies limiting how many pods can be removed per minute, and faster scale-up. I choose a steadier metric, such as requests per second or queue depth, set the CPU requests accurately since utilisation is relative to requests, make sure readiness probes reflect true readiness, and set minReplicas high enough to absorb normal load. Then I test with load to verify.
f: Why is CPU utilisation relative to requests?
What does stabilizationWindowSeconds do?

q: Users see 502 errors for a few seconds on every deployment. How do you make rollouts truly zero-downtime?
p: Traffic is still sent to terminating pods, or new pods receive traffic before they are ready. Add accurate readiness probes, a preStop sleep, SIGTERM handling, enough grace period, a PodDisruptionBudget and sensible maxUnavailable.
tip: Also check keep-alive and idle timeouts on the load balancer, because they can differ from the app's.
a: The 502s mean requests reach a pod that cannot answer. There are two directions. On the way up, a pod may be marked Ready too early, so I make sure the readiness probe checks real dependencies and warm-up, and use a startup probe for slow apps. On the way down, endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen at the same time, so load balancers and the proxy keep sending requests for a few seconds. The fix is a short sleep in a preStop hook, an application that stops accepting new connections and finishes in-flight requests on SIGTERM, and a grace period longer than the longest request. I set maxUnavailable to zero with a surge, add a PodDisruptionBudget, and align load balancer deregistration delay and keep-alive timeouts with the application. Then I verify under load during a rollout, not just in a quiet test.
f: Why does SIGTERM race with endpoint removal?
What should maxUnavailable be for a critical service?

q: The Cluster Autoscaler is not adding nodes even though pods are Pending. How do you investigate?
p: Check why the pods are Pending and whether a new node would help. Common reasons: node group at max size, pod requests larger than any node type, taints or affinity no node group satisfies, quotas, or the autoscaler not discovering the group.
cmds: kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler | grep -i -E 'scale-up|no.*node group'
kubectl get cm cluster-autoscaler-status -n kube-system -o yaml
tip: The status ConfigMap and the pod's TriggeredScaleUp or NotTriggerScaleUp event usually spell out the reason.
a: I begin with a pending pod's events. If I see NotTriggerScaleUp, the message lists why each node group was rejected. Typical reasons are that the node group is already at its maximum size, that the pod requests more CPU or memory than the largest instance type, that node selectors, tolerations or zone constraints match no group, or that a PVC bound to one zone cannot use a group in another zone. Then I read the autoscaler logs and status ConfigMap. Next I check outside Kubernetes: cloud quotas, insufficient capacity for the instance type, launch template errors, and IAM permissions or tags that let the autoscaler discover the group. The fix depends on the cause, such as raising the maximum, adding more instance types, correcting requests, or moving to Karpenter which provisions right-sized nodes directly. I add an alert on pods pending longer than a few minutes.
f: How is Karpenter different in this situation?
Why can PVC zones block scale up?

q: A secret was committed to a Git repository and used in a Kubernetes manifest. What is your response?
p: Treat it as compromised: rotate the credential first, then remove it from the cluster and history, check audit logs and cloud logs for use, and put a control in place such as secret scanning and an external secret manager.
cmds: kubectl get secret app-creds -o yaml | grep -c data
tip: Rewriting Git history is not enough. Anyone who cloned already has it, so rotation is the only real fix.
a: My first action is to revoke and rotate the credential, because once a secret has been pushed I assume it is exposed, even if the repository is private. Next I limit the blast radius: find what the secret grants access to and review the provider's access logs and the cluster audit logs for suspicious use since the commit time. Then I replace it in the cluster with the new value and roll out the workloads that use it. Cleaning history with git filter-repo is good hygiene, but it is not the fix. After the incident I address the root cause: add pre-commit and pipeline secret scanning, stop storing plain secrets in manifests by using External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets, or SOPS with a cloud key management service, prefer workload identity over static keys, and write a short post-incident review so the team learns without blame.
f: How does External Secrets Operator work?
Why prefer workload identity over keys?

q: A developer gets 'forbidden' from kubectl exec. How do you find the missing RBAC permission quickly?
p: Read the error, which names the user, verb, resource and namespace. Use kubectl auth can-i with impersonation, check bindings that reference the user or groups, and remember exec needs create on pods/exec, not just get on pods.
cmds: kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n prod --as dev@corp.com
kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o wide | grep dev@corp.com
tip: For group-based access from OIDC, verify the group claim actually reaches the API server, since bindings to a group do nothing otherwise.
a: The forbidden message is precise: it states which user cannot perform which verb on which resource in which namespace. For exec the resource is the pods/exec subresource with the create verb, which is easy to miss when someone granted only get, list and watch on pods. I confirm with kubectl auth can-i using impersonation, and list everything the user can do with the list flag. Then I check which RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings reference the user or their groups. With single sign-on, I check that the group claim in the token matches the subject name in the binding, as a mismatch is a frequent cause. I then grant the least privilege needed, ideally a Role limited to the namespace and expiring access, and document it in code. For production, I might not allow exec at all, and instead provide ephemeral debug containers with audit.
f: Why is pods/exec a sensitive permission?
How do group claims reach RBAC?

q: Packets are intermittently dropped and dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full'. What do you do?
p: The node's connection tracking table is exhausted, usually by many short connections, high-traffic DNS over UDP, or leaked entries. Raise nf_conntrack_max and hashsize, reduce connection churn, and consider eBPF datapaths that avoid conntrack.
tip: Track the count over max ratio as a node metric and alert on it before drops start.
a: Linux tracks every connection through iptables in a fixed size table. When the table fills, new packets are dropped, which shows up as random timeouts, and the kernel logs table full. On busy Kubernetes nodes this is often caused by many short-lived connections, such as services without keep-alive, high-volume DNS over UDP, or NAT heavy traffic through Services. I check the current count against the maximum and look at which workloads open the most connections. A quick fix is raising nf_conntrack_max and the hash size with sysctl, making sure the node has the memory for it. Real solutions reduce churn: enable connection reuse, add NodeLocal DNSCache, lower unnecessary timeouts, and spread chatty pods across nodes. Cilium with kube-proxy replacement reduces dependence on conntrack. I also add node-level monitoring so we see it coming.
f: Why does DNS over UDP stress conntrack?
How does eBPF reduce conntrack usage?

q: You suspect a memory leak in a service. How do you confirm it from Kubernetes and Prometheus data?
p: Look for a sawtooth that never returns to baseline in container working set memory, restarts with OOMKilled, and a steady upward trend across days. Then use a profiler or heap dump in a staging copy to find the cause.
tip: Use working set, not RSS or usage, since the working set is what the OOM killer compares to the limit.
a: I plot container working set memory per pod over several days and compare it with the memory limit. A leak shows as a rising baseline after each garbage collection or restart, and eventually OOMKilled restarts, visible in the last terminated state. I make sure I'm using working set bytes, because that is the figure the kernel cgroup limit applies to, rather than cache-inclusive usage. I correlate the growth with traffic, deployments and specific endpoints to see what triggers it. Then I move to application level evidence: language runtime metrics like heap size and GC time, heap profiles or dumps taken from a canary, tools like pprof, async-profiler or memory profilers, and look for unbounded caches, goroutine or thread leaks, and unclosed connections. As a mitigation I set a right-sized limit, add a restart policy, and alert on the growth slope, while the code fix is worked on.
f: Why working set rather than usage?
What else besides heap can exceed the limit?

q: Prometheus keeps running out of memory. How do you find the high-cardinality metrics and fix them?
p: Memory scales with active time series. Find the biggest metrics and labels, drop or relabel unbounded labels like user ID or full URL, reduce scrape targets, and shard or move long-term storage to Thanos, Mimir or similar.
tip: The TSDB status page and promtool analyze show the worst offenders in seconds.
a: Prometheus holds the recent data and the index of all active series in memory, so memory grows with series count, which is the product of metrics, label combinations and targets. I start with the TSDB status endpoint or promtool analyze to list the metric names and labels with the most series. The usual cause is a label with unbounded values: user IDs, request paths with IDs inside, pod names in a high churn environment, or histogram buckets multiplied by many labels. Fixes are to remove or normalise those labels in the application, use metric relabeling or drop rules at scrape time, lower the number of scraped targets and histogram buckets, and shorten retention on the local store. For scale I shard by team with several Prometheus instances, use remote write to Thanos, Mimir or a managed service, and enforce series limits per scrape so one team cannot break monitoring.
f: What is cardinality, in one sentence?
How do series limits protect Prometheus?

q: An Argo CD application is stuck OutOfSync or Progressing. How do you diagnose it?
p: OutOfSync means live state differs from Git: check the diff, defaulted fields, and controllers mutating resources. Progressing means health checks have not passed: pods not ready, a hook stuck, or a CRD with no health definition.
tip: Use ignoreDifferences for fields that other controllers legitimately change, such as replicas managed by the HPA.
a: I start with the app diff to see exactly which fields differ. A permanent OutOfSync is often caused by something else mutating the resource: an HPA changing replicas, a mutating webhook injecting sidecars, or API server defaulting that Git does not include. For those I configure ignoreDifferences or respect-ignore-differences rather than fighting it. If the app is Progressing, I look at the resource health tree to see which object is not healthy, such as a Deployment waiting for pods, a Job from a PreSync hook that never completes, or a custom resource without a health check defined. I read the operation state and controller logs for sync errors like invalid manifests, missing CRDs or permission problems. Fixes include correcting the manifest, ordering resources using sync waves, adding custom health checks, and setting retry limits. I also keep a sync window and alerts so problems surface early.
f: What are sync waves and hooks?
Why would an HPA cause OutOfSync?

q: helm upgrade failed and the release is stuck in 'pending-upgrade'. How do you recover?
p: A previous Helm operation was interrupted, leaving a lock-like release status. Check history, roll back to the last deployed revision, or if no rollback is possible remove the stuck release Secret, then fix the chart and upgrade again with --atomic.
tip: Cancelling CI in the middle of a Helm run is the usual cause. Make pipeline jobs non-cancellable during deploy.
a: Helm records each release revision as a Secret, and if an upgrade is interrupted, for example when the pipeline is cancelled or the connection drops, the latest revision can remain in a pending state, and later upgrades report that another operation is in progress. I check the release history to see the revisions and statuses. The preferred recovery is helm rollback to the last good deployed revision, which creates a new revision and clears the problem. If rollback is blocked, I carefully delete the specific stuck revision Secret in the namespace, after backing it up, then rerun the upgrade. Before retrying I find out why the first upgrade failed, using helm template and dry run, and look at pod events. To prevent a repeat I use atomic with a timeout, avoid cancelling deployment jobs, use a concurrency lock in CI, and run helm diff in review.
f: Where does Helm store release data?
What does --atomic do on failure?

q: After a node scale-down or zone issue, pods are packed unevenly and one zone holds most replicas. How do you fix and prevent it?
p: The scheduler only places pods at creation time and does not rebalance. Use topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew, whenUnsatisfiable settings, PodDisruptionBudgets, and optionally the descheduler to rebalance existing pods.
tip: Add minDomains or use nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy in newer versions to make spread behave predictably with autoscaling.
a: Kubernetes schedules a pod only when it is created. After a scale-down, a node failure or a zone event, the replicas that survive stay where they are, so a service can end up concentrated in one zone, which defeats high availability. To fix the current state I can do a rollout restart so the scheduler places new pods with the right constraints, or run the descheduler to evict pods violating spread rules. To prevent it, I add topologySpreadConstraints on the zone and hostname keys with a maxSkew of one, using DoNotSchedule for strict workloads or ScheduleAnyway for flexible ones, together with enough capacity in every zone. I also use PodDisruptionBudgets so draining nodes does not remove too many replicas at once, and make sure the autoscaler has node groups in every zone. Then I test by simulating a zone loss.
f: What does maxSkew mean?
When would you not use DoNotSchedule?

q: Users get 504 Gateway Timeout or 413 errors through the Ingress for certain requests. Where do you look?
p: 504 means the proxy gave up waiting for the backend, so check upstream timeouts and slow pods. 413 means the request body exceeds the proxy limit. Tune per-Ingress annotations, but first find out why the backend is slow.
tip: Raising the timeout hides a slow backend. Check the application latency first and the load balancer idle timeout in front too.
a: I look at the ingress controller logs to see which status, upstream and timing are involved. A 504 means the proxy waited for the upstream longer than its read timeout, 60 seconds by default in NGINX. I check whether the backend is genuinely slow, for example a heavy query or exhausted connection pool, whether pods are overloaded, and whether the cloud load balancer in front of the ingress has its own idle timeout that is shorter. Raising the proxy read timeout for a specific long-running endpoint is acceptable, but I prefer making long operations asynchronous. A 413 means the request body is larger than the proxy body size limit, one megabyte by default in NGINX, so uploads need a higher limit on that Ingress. I change these on specific Ingress objects through annotations, not globally, and I make sure the application and every hop agree.
f: Where else can a timeout be set in the path?
How would you handle large uploads?

q: A cluster upgrade is planned and some manifests use deprecated APIs. How do you avoid breaking workloads?
p: Find the deprecated and removed API versions in use, in live objects and in Git or Helm charts, convert them before upgrading, and upgrade one minor version at a time, with add-ons checked for compatibility.
tip: Check the Kubernetes deprecation guide for each target version. Removals such as PodSecurityPolicy or old Ingress versions have broken real clusters.
a: Before the upgrade I inventory which API versions I use. The API server exposes a metric that counts requests to deprecated APIs, and tools like Pluto and kubent scan live clusters, Helm releases and manifests in Git for removed versions. I read the release notes and deprecation guide for each minor version in the path, since the upgrade must go one minor at a time. I convert the manifests to supported versions, update Helm charts and operators, and check the add-ons such as the CNI, CSI drivers, ingress controller, metrics-server and service mesh for compatibility with the target version. Then I upgrade a non-production cluster first and run smoke tests. For production I back up etcd, upgrade the control plane, then roll the nodes gradually with surge nodes and PodDisruptionBudgets. A written runbook with rollback criteria reduces risk.

q: A Kubernetes Job never finishes, and a CronJob has missed several schedules. How do you troubleshoot?
p: A Job hangs if pods keep failing under backoffLimit, a sidecar keeps running, or the container never exits. A CronJob misses runs because of concurrencyPolicy, startingDeadlineSeconds, suspended state, or too many missed starts.
cmds: kubectl get cronjob nightly -o yaml | grep -E 'suspend|concurrencyPolicy|startingDeadline'
tip: Set activeDeadlineSeconds and ttlSecondsAfterFinished so stuck Jobs terminate and finished ones are cleaned up.
a: For a Job I read its status, the pod events and logs. If pods repeatedly fail, the backoff limit eventually marks the Job failed, so I fix the cause. If the Job stays active, the main container may not exit, or a sidecar such as a proxy never terminates, which the native sidecar feature solves. I add activeDeadlineSeconds so a stuck run is stopped. For a CronJob that misses schedules, I check whether it is suspended, the concurrencyPolicy, since Forbid skips a run if the previous one is still active, and startingDeadlineSeconds. If more than a hundred schedules are missed, the controller stops scheduling and logs an error. Clock and timezone settings also matter. To make batch reliable I make the work idempotent, set history limits and ttlSecondsAfterFinished, send alerts on failed Jobs and on a missing successful run, and make sure resources are sufficient.
